children: By Ira Dugal and Dharamraj Dhutia

India's central bank said on Wednesday it had attracted $136.38 billion in inflows under its forex swap facility as of August 31, bolstering its ability to shield the rupee from shocks, with most of the funds coming through a diaspora-focused dollar deposit scheme.

Indian banks received $127.23 billion through foreign currency deposits by non-residents, $3.89 billion through external commercial borrowings and $5.26 billion through overseas foreign currency borrowings.

In times of currency stress, India has often relied on its diaspora for dollar deposits, offering subsidies on hedging costs as an incentive. The scheme was last used in 2013 and attracted about $26 billion.

In June, the Reserve Bank of India introduced a set of measures, including concessional swap facilities aimed at attracting foreign currency to shore up the rupee, which fell to record lows earlier this year.

"This is clearly larger than expectations. This should give comfort to the RBI on currency, and their ability to manage volatility. Also, it helps understand why they closed the FCNR(B) window earlier than initial schedule," said Vivek Rajpal, Asia strategist at JB Drax Honore (UK).
The dollar deposit scheme was scheduled to close at the end of September, but the central bank chose to end it early on August 31. The window for bank borrowings remains open.
The forex reserves, which rose to a record of $729.33 billion in the week to August 21, will give the RBI more room to shield the rupee from rising oil prices and higher U.S. Treasury yields.
The central bank has stepped up dollar sales to support the rupee over recent days, traders said.
The large inflows could require the RBI to absorb excess rupee liquidity, said Siddharth Kothari, economist at Sunidhi Securities.

"With a record quantum of durable U.S. dollar liquidity entering the system in a relatively compressed time frame, it would be compelling for the RBI to sterilise the resultant INR liquidity through a two-stage approach—an immediate, short-term increase in the Incremental Cash Reserve Ratio (ICRR), followed by a more permanent sterilisation through an increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), or potentially a combination of both," Kothari said.
